title: Three Stories About Being Found
overview: When religious leaders object to Jesus eating with people they see as outsiders, he answers with three stories about something lost, found and celebrated.

parts.label: The complaint (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: Tax collectors gathered money for the Roman occupiers and were widely seen as traitors and cheats, while 'sinners' meant people known for breaking religious law. Sharing a meal signaled friendship and acceptance, so the Pharisees, a group devoted to keeping God's law carefully, and the legal experts took Jesus' table company as approval of these people.

parts.label: The lost sheep (vv. 3-7)
parts.note: The shepherd's search and the party afterward picture God going after one person who has wandered off and rejoicing when they turn back. The mention of ninety-nine good people with no need to turn back may be gently ironic, pointing at the critics themselves, though interpreters read this line in different ways.

parts.label: The lost coin (vv. 8-10)
parts.note: The coin was a silver drachma, worth roughly a day's wage, and in a dim, windowless house finding it meant lighting a lamp and sweeping every corner. The point repeats the first story: heaven shares the joy over one person who turns back.

parts.label: A son leaves home (vv. 11-16)
parts.note: Asking for an inheritance while the father was still alive would have shocked the first listeners as deeply disrespectful. Pigs were unclean under Jewish law, so a Jewish son feeding them and wishing he could eat their food has hit the lowest point imaginable.

parts.label: The father runs (vv. 17-24)
parts.note: In that culture a dignified older man running to meet anyone was unusual, so the father's rush shows love that does not wait for an apology. The robe, ring and sandals mark the son as fully restored as a son, not taken back as a hired worker.

parts.label: The older brother (vv. 25-32)
parts.note: The resentful older son mirrors the critics from verses 1 and 2, who had stayed loyal and now object to the welcome given to others. The story ends without telling us whether he joins the party, leaving the question open for the listeners.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the chapter's main focus is God's welcome of the returning sinner or the challenge to the loyal older brother who resents that welcome.
think: When someone who has done real wrong is welcomed back with celebration, what makes that feel fair or unfair to you?
